headline: California moves to keep A/M licence split as DEA targets state rules
dek: California's regulator filed on 16 November to readopt emergency rules letting retailers split dual licences; a hearing on permanent rules follows on 15 December.
key_points: The Department of Cannabis Control filed with the Office of Administrative Law on 16 November to readopt its emergency rules letting dual-licensed retailers hold a separate medicinal (M) licence.
A parallel rulemaking to make the split permanent takes public comment until 14 December, with a hearing on 15 December.
The new M-licence may sit in a different legal entity, but owners must match, stock must be kept apart and both entities are jointly liable.
DEA's 26 November applicant file lists 779 California entries, but the agency has already questioned whether California's patient rules fit the federal system.
body: California's cannabis regulator is moving to keep alive the licensing workaround it built so that dual-licensed stores could chase federal registration. The Department of Cannabis Control (DCC) filed a package with the state Office of Administrative Law on 16 November to readopt its emergency rules on 'A' and 'M' designations, according to the department's rulemaking page. The rules let a retailer whose single licence covers both adult-use and medicinal sales hold two licences instead, one for each, at the same premises.

The readoption keeps the emergency rules in force while a separate, permanent version works through the normal process. That second package, DCC-2026-04-R, was noticed on 30 October. The department is taking public comment until 14 December and will hold a public hearing on 15 December. Together, the two filings tell operators that California intends this structure to last, even as the federal agency it was built for has signalled doubts about the state's medical programme itself.

The emergency package, DCC-2026-03-E, amends sections 15000.1 and 15000.2 of Title 4 of the California Code of Regulations and adds a new section 15023.1. Only retail licences that carry both designations can use it. A qualifying retailer can ask for its single licence to become an A-licence plus a new M-licence, and the M-licence can be issued to a different legal entity from the one that holds the existing licence.

That flexibility comes with conditions. According to the department's finding of emergency, the two entities must share the same individual owners and the same designated responsible party. Cannabis goods must be physically separated by licence and kept apart in inventory or tracking records. Business records must be kept separately for each licence. And the two entities are jointly and severally liable for all obligations, debts and violations under either licence, so splitting does not shrink anyone's exposure to the state.

There is also a clean-start rule for stock. Existing inventory stays with the existing adult-use licence and its track-and-trace account, and all sales of that inventory run through it. The new M-licence must pay its annual licence fee before inventory moves to it, and the department says it expects the M-licensee to obtain inventory properly rather than simply shifting existing stock across.
> California has built the medical-only shelf DEA asked for. Whether DEA accepts California's definition of a medical patient is a separate question.

The department's finding of emergency lays out the logic plainly. The Attorney General's order of 28 April moved state-licensed medical marijuana to Schedule III and gave applicants 60 days to seek DEA registration under the expedited route. The department lists what registration could bring: relief from Section 280E, which only bites on trafficking in Schedule I or II substances; federal import and export permits; and better access to banking, credit, bankruptcy protection and intellectual property rights.

Without a split, the department wrote, licensees faced a choice between converting to medical-only and losing the adult-use sales they need to survive, or not registering at all. The A/M split was meant to let a medical entity apply while the related adult-use business keeps trading. The department also argued that California, which it calls the largest regulated cannabis market in the world, risked losing ground if out-of-state operators secured registration first.
## DEA's objection is about patients, not paperwork

The structure answers one federal concern but not another. As we reported on 12 November, DEA has sent orders to show cause to applicants in six states and the District of Columbia, beginning the process of denying their applications. The California order, according to the documents Marijuana Moment reviewed, objects that the state lets patients obtain an identification card on the basis of a note in their medical records and treats its written-documentation form as optional. Federal rules adopted with rescheduling treat a state medical certification as equivalent to a prescription only if it is signed and dated and names the patient and a licensed practitioner.

A separate M-licence does not change how California defines a qualifying patient. That is set by state law, not by the DCC's licensing rules. Dentons, in its client alert for the week of 23 November, summarised the show-cause orders as generally citing state rules that allow non-medical sales under the same licence or dispensing without a doctor's written certification. California's split addresses the first problem. The second sits with the legislature.
## How many California businesses are waiting

DEA publishes a daily list of timely applicants, the businesses that filed complete applications in the expedited window and may keep operating under their state licences while they wait. MetaFlora counted the file dated 26 November. It lists 5,752 entries nationwide. California has 779 of them: 488 dispensaries, 209 manufacturers and 82 distributors. Only Oklahoma, with 2,478, has more. When we counted the 11 November file, California had 771.

Those applicants are also living with DEA's separate trading limit, which bars timely applicants from dealing with businesses that are neither registrants nor applicants. A federal appeals court paused that limit on 25 November, four days before it was due to take effect, as we reported on 26 November. The pause is temporary and the court said it is not a ruling on the merits.

First, the Office of Administrative Law's decision on the readoption, which determines whether the emergency rules stay in force without a gap. Second, the 14 December comment deadline and the 15 December hearing on the permanent rules; watch for requests to clarify whether a newly issued M-licence held by a different entity inherits an application filed earlier. Third, how California applicants respond to DEA's show-cause orders, and whether lawmakers move to tighten the state's patient documentation in the 2027 session. Finally, the D.C. Circuit's ruling on the stay requests, which will decide whether the trading limit returns.
